MPG Ranch multimodal survey: robot config

Can seeing a plant from the ground and from the air improve automated species identification? Paired ground-level and overhead imagery of Montana grassland, hand-labeled for 8 plant species, built to answer that question.

8,287labeled ground images
8target species
2sites · 9 strips
1.4 cmRTK accuracy
1.30 cmdrone GSD
33columns

1Contents and motivation

Identifying plant species from photographs is hard from any single vantage point. A camera at ground level sees leaf shape, flower color, and growth habit, but stems overlap and distant plants shrink to a few pixels. A camera looking straight down sees the spatial arrangement of vegetation clearly, but flattens the very structure that distinguishes one species from another. Each view holds information the other lacks. This dataset exists to test whether combining them improves species classification over either alone. A four-legged robot walked lawnmower patterns of parallel legs, nine strips in all, across two grassland sites at MPG Ranch in western Montana, photographing the vegetation ahead of it every meter, with each capture position surveyed to centimeter accuracy. A drone photographed the same ground from above, usually within a few hours of the capture event and always within a day, and its imagery was stitched into a seamless overhead map. Every row of the dataset pairs one ground image with the 4 × 4 m drone image of the ground directly in front of the robot at that moment. A botanist reviewed every one of the 8,287 ground images for the presence of eight target species (four native wildflowers and four invasive weeds) and, in a separate pass, graded each image's quality. Each strip was covered twice, from the ground and the air alike, so the same vegetation appears under two different sets of field conditions.

The two capture events

Every strip was walked twice, and each capture event is paired with its own drone flight. No two capture events see the same conditions. Even at the same clock time, illumination, cloud, wind, and plant posture all differ. The two capture events are best read as two independent condition samples of the same ground rather than a controlled contrast. The interval between them differs by site, and the repeat is spatial rather than exact.

SiteInterval between the two capture eventsCharacter
site_23.0 to 3.4 h, same day Morning and afternoon capture events of the same strip, a within-day contrast
site_148 to 71 h A second capture event two to three days later. Strips 1 and 5 were re-walked at nearly the same time of day

The robot follows the same nominal 1 m grid in both capture events, but it does not land in the same place twice. Matching leg and mark_index across the two capture events, the antenna positions differ by the amounts below.

Separation between the two capture events at the same (leg, mark)Value
median10.1 cm
75th percentile14.9 cm
95th percentile32.6 cm
99th percentile65.6 cm
maximum2.12 m
cumulative
within 10 cm49.0%
within 25 cm91.6%
within 50 cm97.9%
within 1 m99.8%
A (leg, mark_index) pair therefore marks the same neighborhood revisited rather than a fixed quadrat. 4,067 marks appear in both capture events. The remaining 153 appear in only one, where a ground image was skipped in one capture event. Per strip the medians run 6.8 to 14.9 cm and the worst single case is 2.12 m on site_2/strip_1. That is close enough to treat the pair as the same patch of vegetation and too loose to treat it as a fixed plot. The pairing is recorded on every row. pair_frame_id identifies the counterpart ground image, and pair_distance_m, pair_overlap_fraction, and pair_offset_hours quantify the separation.

2Paired examples

The left column shows the robot's ground-level photograph. The right column shows the drone image for the same row, rotated so the robot's bearing points up, with the antenna at the bottom-edge midpoint (yellow).

The drone image is its own coordinate system. Rows are meters ahead of the antenna, columns are meters to the side, and one pixel is exactly 1.30 cm (308 pixels span 4.004 m), so any smaller or repositioned window is plain array slicing with no projection or rotation math (code in section 5). The footprint_wkt column places the 4 m footprint on a map for GIS work. Image work never needs it.

3Splits

The split follows a single rule. The test split is an outermost leg of every strip, leg01 in eight of the nine strips and leg13 in site_1/strip_5, a choice made before the strip's western terminus was recovered in the orthomosaics, and the published split is retained. The assignment was made on geometry, never on the labels. Every other row is a training candidate. Because both capture events walk the same legs, the split groups them automatically, so the same ground never straddles the train/test boundary.

SplitRowsShareDefinition
train6,480 78.2% Zero drone image overlap with any test row
test1,613 19.5% The outermost leg of all 9 strips, both capture events
train_tier_2194 2.3% Its drone image intersects a test drone image. Inclusion is optional

Why train_tier_2 exists

Adjacent legs are 4.1 to 5.3 m apart, and a 4 m drone image reaches 2.0 m laterally, and further once the bearing wanders off the leg axis. So a small number of training drone images cover ground that also appears in a test drone image. Rather than delete them, they are labeled and set aside.

LegRowsWhy it lands in tier 2
leg03126The leg adjacent to a leg01 test leg
leg0244The turn joining leg01 to leg03, whose ground comes within 0.21 m of the test leg. Only 42% of the 106 turn rows qualify. The rest stay in clean train
leg12, leg1016site_1/strip_5: the neighbors of its leg13 test leg
leg05, leg098site_2/strip_2. Its legs run alongside strip_3's test leg where the two strips abut
The zero-overlap guarantee applies to the drone images only. The ground camera is oblique and wide-angle. A train ground image on leg03 shows test-leg terrain 5 m away in essentially every case, at distance and foreshortened. That ground-modality leakage is inherent to the survey geometry and is not quantified. The guarantee is limited to the aerial modality. No drone image in train shares any ground with a test drone image.
Training on train alone is exactly clean in the aerial modality, verified by polygon intersection over every pair of footprints rather than a distance heuristic. Adding train_tier_2 puts 2.50% of the evaluated pixels on ground the model has seen, touching 213 of the 1,613 test drone images. tier2_overlap_fraction supports partial inclusion. The median is 4.5% and the maximum 62.6%, so a threshold recovers most of those rows while leaving the worst behind. This matters most for Euphorbia virgata, the rarest class, which has 11 of its 123 training positives in tier 2.

4Labels

Eight target species, four wildflowers and four weeds, labeled by presence in the ground image. Labels were assigned from a blank slate, with nothing pre-checked and no model predictions shown, by a single annotator per task (one for species, one for artifact_level). No inter-annotator agreement data exists. A ground image with an empty list was reviewed and had no target present (23% of ground images).

The class balance is steep. Poa bulbosa appears in 58.6% of ground images and Euphorbia virgata in 2.1%, a 28× spread. Ground images carry 0 to 6 species at once (median 1), which is why species is a variable-length list rather than a fixed multi-hot vector.

Image quality

A second annotation pass graded every ground image for the share degraded by video decoder artifacts, in four quartile levels numbered 0 to 3 (0-25%, 25-50%, 50-75%, and 75-100% of the image). The robot delivers its camera feed as an H.264 stream over WebRTC, and packets lost on the wireless link leave the decoder to conceal the missing data with content from earlier video frames, which produces blocky or smeared regions. The distribution is U-shaped rather than graded.

The robot's own corruption flag is uninformative here. Every ground image reports corrupt = false, including all 1,304 a human graded at level 3 (75-100% degraded). To select clean imagery, filter on artifact_level.

5Loading the dataset

Basic

# pip install datasets
from datasets import load_dataset

# the clean training split: 6,480 ground images, zero test overlap in the drone images
train = load_dataset("mpg-ranch/multimodal-survey", split="train")
test  = load_dataset("mpg-ranch/multimodal-survey", split="test")

row = train[0]
row["ground_image"]  # PIL.Image, 1280x720: the ground image
row["drone_image"]   # PIL.Image, 308x308: the 4 m nadir drone image, bearing up
row["species"]       # [0, 7]  (class ids, see the multi-hot snippet below)
row["artifact_level"]# 0  (level 0: 0-25% of the ground image degraded)

Species labels to a multi-hot vector

import numpy as np

CLASSES = train.features["species"].feature.names   # canonical order, 8 classes

def multi_hot(batch):
    v = np.zeros((len(batch["species"]), len(CLASSES)), dtype=np.int8)
    for i, ids in enumerate(batch["species"]):
        v[i, ids] = 1                               # species are stored as class ids
    return {"labels": v}

train = train.map(multi_hot, batched=True)

Filtering

# drop the heavily degraded ground images (level 3)
LEVELS = train.features["artifact_level"].names
clean = train.filter(lambda r: r["artifact_level"] != LEVELS.index("75-100%"))

# ground images captured close in time to their drone imagery
tight = train.filter(lambda r: abs(r["capture_offset_time_of_day"]) < 1.0)

# one site, one capture event
morning = train.filter(lambda r: r["site"] == "site_2" and r["capture_event"] == 1)

# rows where a particular species is present
spurge = train.filter(lambda r: CLASSES.index("Euphorbia virgata") in r["species"])

Including tier 2

# all 194 of them: accepts 2.50% evaluated-pixel contamination
t2 = load_dataset("mpg-ranch/multimodal-survey", split="train_tier_2")

# or only the mildly-overlapping ones, e.g. under 10% of the drone image shared
t2_mild = t2.filter(lambda r: r["tier2_overlap_fraction"] < 0.10)

from datasets import concatenate_datasets
train_plus = concatenate_datasets([train, t2_mild])

Using the pair

import torch
from torchvision.transforms.functional import to_tensor

def collate(batch):
    # the ground image is oblique and wide-angle. The drone image is nadir and metric.
    # They cover overlapping ground but are NOT pixel-registered to each other.
    robot = torch.stack([to_tensor(b["ground_image"].resize((640, 360))) for b in batch])
    drone = torch.stack([to_tensor(b["drone_image"]) for b in batch])   # 3x308x308
    y     = torch.tensor(np.stack([b["labels"] for b in batch]), dtype=torch.float32)
    return robot, drone, y

loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(train, batch_size=32, collate_fn=collate)

Re-cropping the drone image

# the drone image is a metric chart: rows are meters ahead of the antenna, columns meters left.
# A smaller or shifted window is array slicing. No projection knowledge is needed.
N, P = 308, 0.0130                              # pixels per side, meters per pixel
PX = 1 / P                                      # 76.9 px per meter

def sub_crop(drone_image, ahead, left, size):
    # (ahead, left): window center in meters from the antenna
    a = np.asarray(drone_image)
    r = round(N - (ahead + size / 2) * PX)      # row 0 is 4.004 m ahead
    c = round(N / 2 - (left + size / 2) * PX)   # column 0 is 2.002 m left
    return a[r : r + round(size * PX), c : c + round(size * PX)]

patch = sub_crop(row["drone_image"], ahead=1.0, left=0.0, size=2.0)  # 2 x 2 m, 154 x 154 px

Recovering the geometry

# each drone image spans 0 to 4.004 m ahead of the antenna and 2.002 m to either side,
# rotated so `bearing_deg` points up the image. To place a drone image pixel on the ground:
import math

def pixel_to_ground(row, px, py, P=0.0130, N=308):
    th = math.radians(row["bearing_deg"])
    fwd = (N - py - 0.5) * P                 # meters ahead of the antenna
    lat = (N / 2 - px - 0.5) * P             # meters to the left
    dE  = fwd * math.sin(th) - lat * math.cos(th)
    dN  = fwd * math.cos(th) + lat * math.sin(th)
    return dE, dN                            # offset in meters, EPSG:6514

6Prior work

Several lines of research connect overhead and ground-level views for organism classification, but only the first below fuses the two as joint classifier input. The others use one view to supervise, label, or direct the other. Releases that combine aerial and ground platforms serve SLAM, registration, navigation, and crop phenotyping. To our knowledge none pairs ground-robot photographs with coincident centimeter-scale drone images cropped from orthomosaics over the same footprints, labeled for plant species in natural vegetation. The closest neighbors follow.

The Auto Arborist Dataset (CVPR 2022)

Pairs aerial and street-level imagery of more than two million urban trees across 23 North American cities for genus-level classification, with baselines for each view alone and for the two combined. It was assembled by joining the cities' public tree censuses to Street View and overhead imagery, and its central experiment is geographic generalization. Models are evaluated in cities held out of training.

TaxaBind (WACV 2025)

Learns a joint embedding over six modalities, using ground-level species photos as the anchor that binds satellite imagery, location, text, audio, and environmental features, and evaluates it on zero-shot species classification. The core technique, multimodal patching, distills each pairwise alignment into the shared ground-image encoder without erasing the ones learned before it, trained on 2.7 million satellite-to-species-photo pairs.

WildSAT (ICCV 2025)

Trains satellite-image encoders by contrasting them against millions of geotagged citizen-science wildlife observations and habitat descriptions, transferring ground-level signal into the overhead view. Its contribution is the training signal itself: a contrastive objective linking a satellite patch to the species recorded there and to Wikipedia habitat text, which beats both ImageNet and satellite-specific pretraining on downstream recognition tasks.

GeoLifeCLEF (annual benchmark)

Predicts plant species composition at ground-observation sites from satellite imagery and environmental rasters, linking the overhead view to species recorded in person at the same coordinates. Recent editions pair roughly five million occurrence records and 100,000 standardized survey plots across Europe with Sentinel-2 patches, Landsat time series, and climate and soil rasters, scored as multi-label species composition prediction.

Aerial-ground robotics for precision farming (IEEE RAM 2021)

The EU Flourish project teamed a survey drone with an intervention ground robot, classifying crops and weeds from both platforms over the same field, the closest operational precedent for the drone-plus-robot pairing here. The demonstrated loop runs from a multispectral drone survey to a weed map co-registered into the ground robot's frame, which the robot then acts on plant by plant with targeted spraying or mechanical stamping.

MuST-C (Scientific Data 2026)

Releases ground-robot photographs and drone orthophotos at millimeter GSD of the same crop plots across a season, co-registered through shared GNSS georeferencing, the closest dataset precedent to the pairing here. The trial is a monoculture experiment where species are known by design, annotations are plant traits rather than species labels, and no per-footprint image pairs are curated.

Outdoor robot imagery datasets (RUGD, RELLIS-3D, GOOSE)

A ground-robot lineage releases outdoor imagery for semantic segmentation. RUGD and RELLIS-3D established the off-road benchmark line, GOOSE carries the finest current ontology at 64 classes, and its GOOSE-Ex extension adds the only annotated quadruped-mounted imagery to date, with vegetation appearing throughout as coarse structural classes such as grass, bush, and tree, never as botanical species.

DeepWeeds (Scientific Reports 2019)

Releases 17,509 ground-level images of eight named weed species across Australian rangeland, the nearest ecosystem and label-type match to this dataset. Capture used a fixed camera rig at robot height rather than a robot in motion, labels are image-level, and no aerial imagery is paired.
